title: Draupadi
body:
Draupadi

यतो धर्मस्ततो जयः सर्वदा संप्रवर्तते।
लक्ष्यं विद्धं शरैरेवमर्जुनस्य महात्मनः॥

"Wherever there is Dharma, there victory will always reside. Thus was the difficult target pierced by the arrows of the high-souled Arjuna."

While in Ekachakra, the Pandavas heard tidings of the magnificent swayamvara of Draupadi, the daughter of King Drupada of Panchala. Reading her sons' silent desire, Kunti gracefully suggested: 'We have stayed in this town long enough; the alms are diminishing, and it is time to move to Drupada's prosperous kingdom.' Travelling to Panchala, they stayed in the cottage of a humble potter, attending the royal assembly in the guise of young Brahmanas. The challenge set by Drupada to win his daughter was extraordinarily difficult: a massive, stiff bow stood in the arena, and high above was a rotating fish target (Matsyayantra) behind a spinning wheel. The archer had to string the bow and shoot five arrows in succession through the wheel to hit the fish's eye, looking only at its reflection in a vessel of oil below.
Mighty kings and warriors—including Duryodhana, Shalya, Shishupala, and Jarasandha—attempted the feat and failed humiliatingly, the stiff bow snapping out of their hands. Even Karna stepped forward, but failed by a hair's breadth. All noises were hushed as Arjuna, disguised in his simple Brahmana deerskin, stepped out from the group of priests. Meditating on Lord Narayana, Arjuna lifted the massive bow with absolute ease, strung it without a tremor, and looking down at the reflection in the oil, sent five arrows in rapid succession through the spinning mechanism, bringing the target down in a storm of celestial flowers and sounding conchs.
Draupadi placed the garland of victory around Arjuna's neck. But when the brothers brought her home to their potter's cottage and called out to Kunti that they had brought 'the most precious alms won today,' Kunti, speaking from inside without looking, commanded: 'Share the alms equally among yourselves.' This maternal command, which could not be revoked, led Draupadi to become the wife of all five brothers. This polyandrous union, while unconventional, served as a profound means of binding the five Pandavas into an unbreakable, unified spiritual unit, preparing them to stand together as a single weapon of Dharma against the upcoming storms of Hastinapur.
